claims.source: ROS-induced activation of TRPA1 has been shown to occur through a process that requires generation of lipid peroxidation products that directly activate the channel, such as 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE) (Sullivan et al., 2015; Trevisani et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sullivan et al., 2015; Trevisani et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Cerebral blood vessels have the inherent ability to dilate in response to hypoxia.
claims.source: Cerebral blood vessels have the inherent ability to dilate in response to hypoxia (Kontos et al., 1978).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kontos et al., 1978.

claims.claim: TRPA1 channels are sensitive to changes in O2 concentration and are activated by both hyperoxic and hypoxic conditions.
claims.source: Although the molecular and cellular mechanisms responsible for this important response are not known, a recent study suggested that TRPA1 channels are sensitive to changes in O2 concentration and are activated by both hyperoxic and hypoxic conditions (Takahashi et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Takahashi et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Hypoxia and ischemia are linked to elevated ROS production and increased generation of 4-HNE.
claims.source: In addition, hypoxia and ischemia are linked to elevated ROS production and increased generation of 4-HNE (Schmidt et al., 1996; Kunstmann et al., 1996), an endogenous activator of TRPA1 activity.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schmidt et al., 1996; Kunstmann et al., 1996.

claims.claim: 4-HNE significantly increased the frequency of TRPA1 sparklets in cerebral artery endothelial cells from Tek:Gcamp6f mice.
claims.source: We observed that 4-HNE significantly increased the frequency of highly localized, transient Ca2+ signals by approximately 10-fold compared with vehicle controls (0.51 ± 0.05 Hz vs. 0.07 ± 0.01 Hz) (Figure 1D and Videos 5 and 6).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1D and Videos 5 and 6, showing measurements of Ca2+ signal frequency.

claims.claim: The selective TRPA1 antagonist A967079 significantly diminished the 4-HNE–induced increase in Ca2+ signal frequency.
claims.source: The selective TRPA1 antagonist A967079 (1 μM) (Chen et al., 2011) significantly diminished the 4-HNE–induced increase in activity, reducing the frequency of these Ca2+ signals from 0.51 ± 0.06 Hz to 0.06 ± 0.02 Hz (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1E and a citation to Chen et al., 2011 for the antagonist.

claims.claim: The number of active TRPA1 sparklet sites per field of view significantly increased from 1.68 ± 0.27 under control conditions to 4.41 ± 0.52 in the presence of 4-HNE.
claims.source: Further analyses showed that the number of active sites per field of view significantly increased from 1.68 ± 0.27 under control conditions to 4.41 ± 0.52 in the presence of 4-HNE (Figure 1B and D, data shown as number of sites per cell).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1B and D.

claims.claim: TRPA1 sparklet frequency at existing sites significantly increased from 0.06 ± 0.01 Hz at baseline to 0.13 ± 0.02 Hz following application of 4-HNE.
claims.source: In addition, sparklet frequency at existing sites significantly increased from 0.06 ± 0.01 Hz at baseline to 0.13 ± 0.02 Hz following application of 4-HNE (Figure 1C and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1C and D.

claims.claim: The mean attack time of mode-amplitude TRPA1 sparklets was 87 ± 7 ms.
claims.source: The mean attack time (half-time to reach peak signal amplitude), decay time (half-time from peak to loss of signal), and duration of mode-amplitude TRPA1 sparklets were 87 ± 7 ms, 84 ± 6 ms, and 373 ± 23 ms, respectively.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements reported in the text.

claims.claim: The mean spatial spread of TRPA1 sparklets was approximately 17.2 ± 0.6 μm2.
claims.source: The mean spatial spread of TRPA1 sparklets was approximately 17.2 ± 0.6 μm2, or ~3% of the total surface area of a single endothelial cell in this intact vascular preparation (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements reported in the text and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: 4-HNE significantly increased the frequency of Ca2+ transients in cerebral artery endothelial cells in the absence of CPA or EGTA-AM.
claims.source: 4-HNE significantly increased the frequency of Ca2+ transients (0.76 ± 0.08 vs. 2.44 ± 0.20 Hz, Videos 7 and 8, Figure 2C), and this response was blocked by the TRPA1 channel inhibitor A967079 (1.12 ± 0.09 Hz, Figure 2C and Video 9).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2C and Videos 7, 8, and 9.

claims.claim: Hypoxia increased 4-HNE immunolabeling in cerebral arteries compared to normoxic conditions.
claims.source: We observed an increase in 4-HNE immunolabeling in cerebral arteries superfused with hypoxic PSS when compared to arteries superfused with normoxic PSS (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Acute hypoxic exposure significantly increased the frequency of TRPA1 sparklets in cerebral artery endothelial cells.
claims.source: Acute hypoxic exposure significantly increased the frequency of TRPA1 sparklets, a response that was significantly reduced by A967079 (Figure 3B–3D and Videos 10 and 11).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B–3D and Videos 10 and 11.

claims.claim: Hypoxia-induced increases in TRPA1 sparklet frequency were not significantly inhibited by extracellular superoxide dismutase (SOD) and the NOX inhibitor apocynin.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, we found that extracellular superoxide dismutase (SOD) and the NOX inhibitor apocynin did not significantly inhibit hypoxia-induced increases in TRPA1 sparklet frequency (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting the involvement of an alternative pathway.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Hypoxia-induced increases in TRPA1 sparklet frequency and sites per cell were significantly reduced by membrane-permeant PEG-SOD.
claims.source: Consistent with this latter possibility, we found that hypoxia-induced increases in TRPA1 sparklet frequency and sites per cell were significantly reduced by membrane-permeant PEG-SOD, suggesting that intracellular generation of ROS is essential for this response (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Hypoxia caused a time-dependent increase in the fluorescence intensity of the ROS indicator dihydroethidium (DHE) in freshly isolated cerebral artery endothelial cells.
claims.source: This conclusion is supported by imaging experiments showing that hypoxia caused a time-dependent increase in the fluorescence intensity of the ROS indicator dihydroethidium (DHE) in freshly isolated cerebral artery endothelial cells, which was prevented by PEG-SOD (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data presented in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Pre-incubation with the mitochondrial-targeted antioxidant mitoTEMPO significantly inhibited hypoxia-induced increases in DHE fluorescence.
claims.source: In agreement with this report, we found that pre-incubation of freshly isolated endothelial cells with the mitochondrial-targeted antioxidant mitoTEMPO (500 nM) significantly inhibited hypoxia-induced increases in DHE fluorescence (Figure 4A), suggesting that mitochondria are the primary source of intracellular ROS generated during hypoxia.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Treatment with mitoTEMPO significantly diminished hypoxia-induced increases in TRPA1 sparklet frequency.
claims.source: To determine if mitochondrial ROS are responsible for the activation of TRPA1 channels during hypoxia, we treated cerebral arteries from Tek:Gcamp6f mice with mitoTEMPO prior to hypoxia exposure. This treatment significantly diminished hypoxia-induced increases in TRPA1 sparklet frequency, indicating a critical role for mitochondrial ROS generation in this response (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Acute exposure to hypoxia induced vasodilation of cerebral pial arteries that was significantly diminished by disruption of endothelial cell function.
claims.source: Arteries were pressurized to physiological levels (60 mmHg) and allowed to generate spontaneous myogenic tone. Acute exposure to hypoxia (pO2 = 13 ± 2 mmHg) induced vasodilation that was significantly diminished by disruption of endothelial cell function by passing an air bubble through the vascular lumen (Ralevic et al., 1989) (Figure 5A), indicating involvement of the endothelium.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5A and a citation to Ralevic et al., 1989 for the method.

claims.claim: Vasodilation in response to hypoxia was inhibited by Tempol.
claims.source: Vasodilation in response to hypoxia was also inhibited by Tempol (100 µM) (Figure 5B), but was not significantly reduced by NOX2 inhibition and extracellular SOD (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), supporting the concept that intracellular ROS generation is required for this response.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Hypoxia-induced dilation was significantly blunted by mitoTEMPO.
claims.source: Further, we found that hypoxia-induced dilation was significantly blunted by mitoTEMPO (500 nM) (Figure 5C), suggesting that mitochondria are the source of ROS required for this response.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Vasodilation in response to hypoxic exposure was significantly reduced by blockade of TRPA1 channels with A967079.
claims.source: Vasodilation in response to hypoxic exposure was significantly reduced by blockade of TRPA1 channels with A967079 (Figure 6A) and was diminished in cerebral arteries isolated from endothelial cell-specific TRPA1 knockout mice (Trpa1 ecKO) (Sullivan et al., 2015) compared with TRPA1 floxed, cre-recombinase negative, littermate controls (Trpa1fl/fl, Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6A and 6B, and a citation to Sullivan et al., 2015 for the mouse model.

claims.claim: Hypoxia-induced dilation was diminished in cerebral arteries isolated from endothelial cell-specific TRPA1 knockout mice (Trpa1 ecKO) compared with TRPA1 floxed, cre-recombinase negative, littermate controls (Trpa1fl/fl).
claims.source: Vasodilation in response to hypoxic exposure was significantly reduced by blockade of TRPA1 channels with A967079 (Figure 6A) and was diminished in cerebral arteries isolated from endothelial cell-specific TRPA1 knockout mice (Trpa1 ecKO) (Sullivan et al., 2015) compared with TRPA1 floxed, cre-recombinase negative, littermate controls (Trpa1fl/fl, Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6B and a citation to Sullivan et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Blockade of KCa3.1 channels with TRAM34 and KCa2.3 channels with apamin significantly reduced hypoxia-induced dilation.
claims.source: To investigate potential vasodilator mechanisms acting downstream of TRPA1 channels, we blocked KCa3.1 channels with TRAM34 and KCa2.3 channels with apamin. This treatment significantly reduced hypoxia-induced dilation (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: TRPA1 immunofluorescence was detected in the endothelium of penetrating arterioles.
claims.source: TRPA1 immunofluorescence was detected in the endothelium of penetrating arterioles (Figure 7A, left panels, red) but was not detected when the primary antibody for TRPA1 was omitted, although GFP fluorescence was observed (Figure 7A, right panels).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Exposing penetrating arterioles to 4-HNE induced dilation that was significantly diminished by A967079.
claims.source: Functional ex vivo pressure myography experiments showed that exposing penetrating arterioles to 4-HNE induced dilation that was significantly diminished by A967079 (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Exposure of pressurized penetrating arterioles to hypoxia caused dilation that was blunted by A967079.
claims.source: In addition, exposure of pressurized penetrating arterioles to hypoxia caused dilation that was blunted by A967079 (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Infarct size was significantly increased in Trpa1 ecKO mice compared with littermate controls 24 hr after MCAO.
claims.source: We found that although reduction in cerebral perfusion after MCAO did not significantly differ between Trpa1fl/fl and Trpa1 ecKO mice (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), infarct size was significantly increased in Trpa1 ecKO mice compared with littermate controls 24 hr after MCAO (Figure 8A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Pharmacological activation of TRPA1 channels in vivo by intraperitoneal injection of cinnamaldehyde (CinA, 50 mg/kg), administered 15 min after MCAO, significantly reduced infarct size in control C57/bl6 mice.
claims.source: Pharmacological activation of TRPA1 channels in vivo by intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of CinA (50 mg/kg) (Huang et al., 2007), administered 15 min after MCAO, significantly reduced infarct size in control C57/bl6 mice (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8B and a citation to Huang et al., 2007 for the dosage.

claims.claim: The protective effect of CinA on infarct size is partially dependent on endothelial cell TRPA1 channels as infarct size in Trpa1 ecKO mice was not significantly reduced by CinA.
claims.source: This protective effect of CinA is partially dependent on endothelial cell TRPA1 channels as infarct size in Trpa1 ecKO mice was not significantly reduced by CinA (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: TRPA1 channels are activated by electrophilic compounds, such as AITC, allicin and CinA, which target specific cysteine residues located in the cytosolic pre-S1 domain.
claims.source: TRPA1 channels are activated by electrophilic compounds, such as AITC, allicin and CinA, which target specific cysteine residues located in the cytosolic pre-S1 domain linking the channel's ankyrin-repeat region to the first membrane-spanning domain (Hinman et al., 2006; Macpherson et al., 2007; Paulsen et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hinman et al., 2006; Macpherson et al., 2007; Paulsen et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Lipid peroxidation products such as 4-HNE act on the same cysteine residues that are targeted by electrophilic molecules.
claims.source: Lipid peroxidation products such as 4-HNE and related substances appear to act on the same cysteine residues that are targeted by electrophilic molecules (Hinman et al., 2006; Macpherson et al., 2007; Pires and Earley, 2017), providing evidence for a common mechanism of activation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hinman et al., 2006; Macpherson et al., 2007; Pires and Earley, 2017.

claims.claim: The pO2 in the rat brain following an ischemic stroke varies from near anoxia in the infarct core (~1–2 mmHg) to ~10–15 mmHg in the peri-infarct area.
claims.source: It should be noted that the pO2 in the rat brain following an ischemic stroke varies from near anoxia in the infarct core (~1–2 mmHg) to ~10–15 mmHg in the peri-infarct area (Liu et al., 2004) — values of pO2 similar to those observed in our tissue bath experiments.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2004.

claims.claim: Acute hypoxic exposure uncouples the mitochondrial electron transport chain, stimulating a localized burst of O2-.
claims.source: Previous reports have shown that acute hypoxic exposure uncouples the mitochondrial electron transport chain (Klimova and Chandel, 2008), stimulating a localized burst of O2- (Hernansanz-Agustín et al., 2014), which can enter the cytoplasm through anion channels present in the mitochondrial outer membrane (Han et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Klimova and Chandel, 2008; Hernansanz-Agustín et al., 2014; Han et al., 2003.

claims.claim: Hypoxia increases mitochondrial O2- production in cancer cells and cultured endothelial cells.
claims.source: In agreement with earlier reports showing that hypoxia increases mitochondrial O2- production in cancer cells (Chandel et al., 2000; Sabharwal and Schumacker, 2014; Eales et al., 2016) and cultured endothelial cells (Hernansanz-Agustín et al., 2014), we found that exposure to acute hypoxia stimulated ROS generation in native cerebral artery endothelial cells, and that this response was inhibited by a mitochondrial-targeted SOD mimetic and by intracellular PEG-SOD.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chandel et al., 2000; Sabharwal and Schumacker, 2014; Eales et al., 2016; Hernansanz-Agustín et al., 2014, and experimental data from the study.

claims.claim: Mitochondria are located at the base of myoendothelial projections.
claims.source: A recent study reported that mitochondria are located at the base of myoendothelial projections (Maarouf et al., 2017), which are regions of near contact between the plasma membrane of endothelial cells and the underlying smooth muscle cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Maarouf et al., 2017.

claims.claim: TRPA1 channels are concentrated within myoendothelial projections.
claims.source: TRPA1 channels are also concentrated within myoendothelial projection (Sullivan et al., 2015; Earley et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sullivan et al., 2015; Earley et al., 2009.

claims.claim: TRPA1 channels conduct mixed cation currents with a large Ca2+ fraction.
claims.source: TRPA1 channels conduct mixed cation currents with a large Ca2+ fraction (Karashima et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2008), and activation of TRPA1 on the plasma membrane of endothelial cells transiently creates small microdomains with high localized Ca2+ concentrations (Sullivan et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Karashima et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2008; Sullivan et al., 2015.

claims.claim: TRPA1-mediated Ca2+ influx stimulated by direct application of AITC or through O2- generated by NOX2 triggers endothelium-dependent dilation of cerebral arteries.
claims.source: Our prior studies demonstrated that TRPA1-mediated Ca2+ influx stimulated by direct application of AITC (Earley et al., 2009) or through O2- generated by NOX2 (1) triggers endothelium-dependent dilation of cerebral arteries, a response that is unaffected by blocking nitric oxide synthase or cyclooxygenase pathways, but is sensitive to inhibition of Ca2+-activated KCa3.1 and KCa2.3 K+ channels.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Earley et al., 2009 and reference (1), and prior experimental work.

claims.claim: TRPA1 channels and KCa3.1 channels co-localize within myoendothelial projections.
claims.source: TRPA1 channels and KCa3.1 channels co-localize within myoendothelial projections (Earley et al., 2009), such that influx of Ca2+ though TRPA1 channels within these spatially restricted regions is sufficient to increase the local [Ca2+] to levels capable of activating outward K+ currents through KCa3.1 and KCa2.3, leading to hyperpolarization of the endothelial cell plasma membrane (Sullivan et al., 2015; Earley et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Earley et al., 2009; Sullivan et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Hyperpolarization of the endothelial cell plasma membrane is conducted to SMCs through myoendothelial gap junctions, resulting in relaxation and vasodilation.
claims.source: Hyperpolarization of the endothelial cell plasma membrane, in turn, is conducted to SMCs through myoendothelial gap junctions, resulting in relaxation and vasodilation (Sokoya et al., 2006; Chadha et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sokoya et al., 2006; Chadha et al., 2011.

claims.claim: TRPA1 activation by AITC and 4-HNE stimulates Ca2+ release from intracellular stores.
claims.source: In addition, TRPA1 activation by AITC (Qian et al., 2013) and 4-HNE stimulates Ca2+ release from intracellular stores, leading to an increase in Ca2+ transients previously linked to activation of KCa3.1 (39).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Qian et al., 2013 and reference (39).

claims.claim: TRPV3 has been shown to be sensitized by acute hypoxia in a ROS-independent manner.
claims.source: Several possibilities have been reported, including endogenous generation of carbon monoxide (Leffler et al., 1999) and TRPV3 channel activity. TRPV3 has been shown to be sensitized by acute hypoxia in a ROS-independent manner (Karttunen et al., 2015), and cause endothelium-dependent dilation of cerebral pial arteries and penetrating arterioles in response to chemical agonists (Pires et al., 2015; Earley et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Karttunen et al., 2015; Pires et al., 2015; Earley et al., 2010.

claims.claim: The extent of neuronal loss following an ischemic insult is determined in part by the supply of blood to the region surrounding the infarct core, known as the ischemic penumbra.
claims.source: The extent of neuronal loss following an ischemic insult is determined in part by the supply of blood to the region surrounding the infarct core, known as the ischemic penumbra (Maas et al., 2009; Hoehn-Berlage et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Maas et al., 2009; Hoehn-Berlage et al., 1995.

claims.claim: The penumbra is characterized by structurally intact, but metabolic silent, parenchymal tissue in which perfusion is impaired.
claims.source: The penumbra is characterized by structurally intact, but metabolic silent, parenchymal tissue in which perfusion is impaired (Symon et al., 1977).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Symon et al., 1977.

claims.claim: Increasing blood flow to the ischemic penumbra has been shown to reduce expansion of the infarct zone and improve neurological outcomes.
claims.source: Increasing blood flow to the ischemic penumbra has been shown to reduce expansion of the infarct zone and, consequently, improve neurological outcomes (Cipolla et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cipolla et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Isoflurane was previously shown to potentiate TRPA1 activity.
claims.source: Isoflurane, the anesthetic agent used during MCAO surgeries, was previously shown to potentiate TRPA1 activity (Matta et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Matta et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Isoflurane anesthesia is neuroprotective in various animal models of stroke and subarachnoid hemorrhage.
claims.source: Interestingly, isoflurane anesthesia is neuroprotective in various animal models of stroke and subarachnoid hemorrhage (Altay et al., 2012a; Altay et al., 2012b; Li et al., 2013; Khatibi et al., 2011), but the mechanistic basis of this effect is not known.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Altay et al., 2012a; Altay et al., 2012b; Li et al., 2013; Khatibi et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Tek:Gcamp6f mice were generated by crossing mice heterozygous for the expression of a floxed Stop codon upstream of the Gcamp6f gene with mice heterozygous for the expression of cre-recombinase under the control of the endothelial-specific Tek promoter/enhancer (Tekcre).
claims.source: To accomplish this, we crossed mice heterozygous for the expression of a floxed Stop codon upstream of the Gcamp6f gene (see Materials and methods) with mice heterozygous for the expression of cre-recombinase under the control of the endothelial-specific Tek promoter/enhancer (Tekcre).
claims.evidence: The claim describes the experimental method used to generate the Tek:Gcamp6f mouse line.

claims.claim: The mT/mG reporter mouse was used to confirm that cre-recombinase is only expressed in the endothelium of cerebral arteries from Tekcre mice.
claims.source: The mT/mG reporter mouse (Muzumdar et al., 2007) was used to confirm that cre-recombinase is only expressed in the endothelium of cerebral arteries from Tekcre mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and a citation to Muzumdar et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Cerebral, mesenteric, skeletal muscle and pulmonary arteries isolated from Tek:Gcamp6f mice expressed the Ca2+ biosensor only in the endothelium.
claims.source: We found that cerebral, mesenteric, skeletal muscle and pulmonary arteries isolated from Tek:Gcamp6f mice expressed the Ca2+ biosensor only in the endothelium and provided excellent signal-to-noise ratio for optical detection of spontaneous and evoked Ca2+ signals in this tissue (Videos 1–4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and Videos 1–4.

claims.claim: The pO2 measured in the recording bath under hypoxic conditions was 13 ± 2 mmHg.
claims.source: Hypoxia was achieved by superfusing the tissue with physiological saline solution (PSS) equilibrated with a hypoxic gas mixture (5% O2, 6% CO2, 89% N2). The pO2 measured in the recording bath under these conditions was 13 ± 2 mmHg (n = 5).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements reported in the text.

claims.claim: The pH of the superfusing solution was constantly maintained between 7.37 and 7.42 during normoxic and hypoxic conditions.
claims.source: The pH of the superfusing solution was monitored in real time, and was constantly maintained between 7.37 and 7.42 during normoxic and hypoxic conditions.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental monitoring reported in the text.

claims.claim: Hypoxia causes activation of TRPA1 channels in the cerebral endothelium, resulting in vasodilation.
claims.source: Here, we tested the hypothesis that hypoxia causes activation of TRPA1 channels in the cerebral endothelium, resulting in vasodilation, and further propose that this response constitutes an adaptive response during perfusion deficiency.
claims.evidence: This is the main hypothesis being tested in the study.

claims.claim: TRPA1 channels in the cerebral endothelium are early sensors of hypoxia and initiate an adaptive response to reduce ischemic damage in the brain.
claims.source: Our findings suggest that TRPA1 channels in the cerebral endothelium are early sensors of hypoxia and initiate an adaptive response to reduce ischemic damage in the brain.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claims.claim: Endothelial TRPA1 channels are sensors of hypoxia leading to vasodilation, thereby reducing ischemic damage.
claims.source: These data suggest that endothelial TRPA1 channels are sensors of hypoxia leading to vasodilation, thereby reducing ischemic damage.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the study's findings.

claims.claim: Hypoxia-induced activation of TRPA1 in the cerebral endothelium constitutes a novel adaptive response.
claims.source: Selective deletion of TRPA1 expression in the endothelium exacerbated the loss of brain tissue associated with ischemic stroke, providing evidence that hypoxia-induced activation of TRPA1 in the cerebral endothelium constitutes a novel adaptive response.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claims.claim: Activation of TRPA1 channels in endothelial cells of cerebral arteries is an early adaptive response to acute reduction in tissue pO2, leading to a possible increase in perfusion within the penumbra.
claims.source: Our findings suggest that activation of TRPA1 channels in endothelial cells of cerebral arteries is an early adaptive response to acute reduction in tissue pO2, leading to a possible increase in perfusion within the penumbra.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claims.claim: Isoflurane may provide neuroprotection by potentiating TRPA1-mediated cerebral arterial dilation.
claims.source: The current findings support the concept that isoflurane may provide neuroprotection by potentiating TRPA1-mediated cerebral arterial dilation.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the study's findings and prior knowledge about isoflurane.

claims.claim: Hypoxia may induce generation of 4-HNE within myoendothelial projections, leading to TRPA1 activation in those sites.
claims.source: A recent study reported that mitochondria are located at the base of myoendothelial projections (Maarouf et al., 2017), which are regions of near contact between the plasma membrane of endothelial cells and the underlying smooth muscle cells. TRPA1 channels are also concentrated within myoendothelial projection (Sullivan et al., 2015; Earley et al., 2009). Thus, it is possible that hypoxia-induced increases in mitochondria O2- production generates 4-HNE within myoendothelial projections, leading to TRPA1 activation in those sites.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the spatial localization of mitochondria and TRPA1 channels.

results.result: The authors generated a novel transgenic mouse line (Tek:Gcamp6f) that expresses the Ca2+ biosensor Gcamp6f exclusively in endothelial cells by crossing floxed Gcamp6f mice with Tek-cre mice. This mouse line was validated using mT/mG reporter mice and showed endothelial-specific expression in multiple arterial beds.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57 describe the generation and validation of the Tek:Gcamp6f mouse model. The breeding strategy is clearly described (C55), validated using reporter mice (C56), and functional expression confirmed in multiple vascular beds (C57). The experimental approach is sound and appropriately controlled.

results.result: 4-HNE significantly increased TRPA1 sparklet frequency (~10-fold) in cerebral artery endothelial cells, which was blocked by the selective TRPA1 antagonist A967079. The increase resulted from both recruitment of new sparklet sites and increased frequency at existing sites. TRPA1 sparklets had characteristic kinetics (attack time 87±7 ms) and spatial spread (~17.2±0.6 μm²).
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C16 provide comprehensive characterization of 4-HNE-induced TRPA1 sparklets with quantitative data, appropriate controls (A967079), and detailed biophysical parameters. The ~10-fold increase in frequency with pharmacological blockade provides strong evidence for TRPA1-mediated Ca2+ influx. Statistical significance is reported.

results.result: In the absence of EGTA-AM and CPA, 4-HNE significantly increased the frequency of larger Ca2+ transients in cerebral artery endothelial cells, which was blocked by A967079.
results.evaluation: Claim C17 demonstrates that TRPA1 activation triggers Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release from intracellular stores when ER Ca2+ is not depleted. The experimental design appropriately removes pharmacological agents that would prevent ER Ca2+ release, and the A967079 blockade confirms TRPA1 dependence.

results.result: Hypoxia (pO2 ~13 mmHg) increased 4-HNE immunolabeling and significantly increased TRPA1 sparklet frequency in cerebral artery endothelial cells, which was blocked by A967079.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C19 establish that pathophysiologically relevant hypoxia increases both 4-HNE production and TRPA1 activity. The immunofluorescence data (C18) and functional Ca2+ imaging (C19) provide complementary evidence. The pO2 was carefully monitored and maintained at physiologically relevant levels.

results.result: Hypoxia-induced TRPA1 activation requires intracellular, mitochondrial-derived ROS rather than extracellular NOX2-derived superoxide. Hypoxia increased DHE fluorescence in endothelial cells, which was prevented by membrane-permeant PEG-SOD and the mitochondrial-targeted antioxidant mitoTEMPO. MitoTEMPO also significantly reduced hypoxia-induced TRPA1 sparklet frequency.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C24 systematically identify mitochondria as the ROS source during hypoxia using appropriate pharmacological tools (extracellular SOD, apocynin, PEG-SOD, mitoTEMPO) and DHE imaging. The negative results with NOX inhibitors (C20) and positive results with mitochondrial-targeted interventions (C23-C24) provide strong mechanistic evidence.

results.result: Hypoxia induced endothelium-dependent vasodilation of cerebral pial arteries that was inhibited by endothelial denudation, the antioxidant Tempol, and the mitochondrial-targeted antioxidant mitoTEMPO.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27 demonstrate that hypoxia-induced vasodilation requires functional endothelium and mitochondrial ROS. The use of endothelial denudation (C25) and selective antioxidants (C26-C27) provides appropriate controls. However, the endothelial denudation method (air bubble) could potentially cause non-specific damage.

results.result: Hypoxia-induced vasodilation of cerebral arteries was significantly reduced by TRPA1 blockade with A967079, diminished in Trpa1 ecKO mice, and significantly reduced by blockade of KCa3.1 and KCa2.3 channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C30 establish TRPA1 and downstream K+ channels as mediators of hypoxia-induced vasodilation using both pharmacological (A967079, TRAM34, apamin) and genetic (Trpa1 ecKO) approaches. The convergent evidence from multiple approaches strengthens the conclusion, though the incomplete blockade suggests additional mechanisms may contribute.

results.result: TRPA1 channels are present in penetrating arterioles and mediate vasodilation in response to both 4-HNE and hypoxia, as shown by immunofluorescence and pressure myography experiments with A967079 blockade.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C33 extend the findings from pial arteries to penetrating arterioles using immunofluorescence (C31) and functional pressure myography (C32-C33). The appropriate negative control (primary antibody omission) and pharmacological blockade support the conclusions.

results.result: Endothelial TRPA1 channels are neuroprotective during ischemic stroke. Infarct size was significantly increased in Trpa1 ecKO mice compared to controls 24 hr after MCAO. Pharmacological TRPA1 activation with cinnamaldehyde (50 mg/kg i.p.) reduced infarct size in wildtype mice but not in Trpa1 ecKO mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36 demonstrate the in vivo relevance of endothelial TRPA1 using both loss-of-function (Trpa1 ecKO) and gain-of-function (CinA treatment) approaches in the MCAO model. The lack of CinA effect in Trpa1 ecKO mice (C36) confirms endothelial TRPA1 dependence. Cerebral perfusion was monitored and did not differ between genotypes, strengthening the conclusion.

results.result: The experimental hypoxia conditions were carefully controlled and monitored, with pO2 maintained at 13±2 mmHg and pH maintained between 7.37-7.42 during both normoxic and hypoxic conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 describe critical experimental parameters that were appropriately monitored. The pO2 levels achieved are pathophysiologically relevant (similar to peri-infarct regions in stroke), and pH control rules out acidosis as a confounding factor. This methodological rigor strengthens all hypoxia-related findings.

results.result: The authors conclude that TRPA1 channels in cerebral endothelial cells function as early sensors of hypoxia, leading to vasodilation that reduces ischemic damage in the brain, constituting a novel adaptive response.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C73 represent the main conclusions of the study. These are well-supported by the convergent evidence from Ca2+ imaging (C11-C24), pressure myography (C25-C33), and in vivo stroke experiments (C34-C36). The mechanistic pathway from hypoxia → mitochondrial ROS → 4-HNE → TRPA1 → KCa channels → vasodilation is systematically established.

results.result: The authors speculate that isoflurane may provide neuroprotection by potentiating TRPA1-mediated cerebral arterial dilation.
results.evaluation: Claim C74 is speculative and based on prior literature showing isoflurane potentiates TRPA1 (C53) and is neuroprotective (C54). However, no direct experimental evidence is provided in this study to test this hypothesis. This remains an interesting but unvalidated speculation requiring future work.

results.result: The authors propose that hypoxia-induced mitochondrial ROS generation may produce 4-HNE within myoendothelial projections where TRPA1 channels are concentrated, leading to localized TRPA1 activation.
results.evaluation: Claim C75 is a mechanistic speculation based on the spatial colocalization of mitochondria (C42) and TRPA1 channels (C43) at myoendothelial projections. While plausible, the study does not directly demonstrate 4-HNE production specifically at these sites or measure local TRPA1 activity within myoendothelial projections during hypoxia. This hypothesis requires direct experimental validation.
